mapper.verbatim_quote:
must not:
(a) hold the records, or take the records, outside Australia; or
(b) process or handle the information relating to the records outside Australia
mapper.rationale: Sectoral (health records) local processing/holding mandate under My Health Records Act -> category (2) => 0.5, per Australia precedent.

verifier.reason: Section 77(1) imposes a ban on holding, taking, processing or handling health records outside Australia. This is a local processing requirement (processing = collection, organization, structuring, storage, adaptation, use, disclosure, dissemination per Guide p.50). It applies to a SPECIFIC SECTOR (health/My Health Record system) and a SPECIFIC DATA TYPE (health records only), not horizontally across all sectors or to personal data generally. One sectoral measure = scoring tree branch 0.5. Not a 6.4 conditional-flow trap: the provision contains an outright ban with narrow exception (s.77(2)) for system operation, not a default-permission-with-conditions regime.

mapper.verbatim_quote:
must not:
(a) hold the records, or take the records, outside Australia
mapper.rationale: Same provision also mandates local storage of health records; dual-recording rule applies, sectoral -> 0.5.

verifier.reason: Section 77(1) mandates that System Operators, registered repository/portal operators, and contracted service providers must not "hold the records...outside Australia" or "process or handle the information relating to the records outside Australia." This is a dual requirement combining local processing (subsection b) and implicitly local storage (subsection a). Under 6.2, the ban on holding/processing outside Australia constitutes a LOCAL STORAGE REQUIREMENT (records must be retained domestically). Since this applies to a SPECIFIC SECTOR and SPECIFIC DATA TYPE (My Health Records system personal data only, not personal data generally), it falls under the ONE measure applied to specific sector/data category branch, scoring 0.5. TRAP CHECK: This is NOT a conditional-flow regime (6.4)—it is an absolute prohibition with no compliant transfer pathway. The subsection (2) exemption for system operation does not override the sectoral scope classification. DUAL-RECORDING NOTE: Subsection (b) references "process...outside Australia," which could trigger 6.1 (local processing requirement), but the primary and controlling requirement is the ban on holding records outside the country, which is a storage mandate per 6.2 definition.

mapper.verbatim_quote: the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the overseas recipient does not breach the Australian Privacy Principles (other than Australian Privacy Principle 1) in relation to the information
mapper.rationale: APP 8 imposes a horizontal accountability condition on cross-border disclosure of personal data (with exceptions in 8.2) - conditional flow regime covering personal data horizontally scores 1

verifier.reason: APP 8.1 imposes a CONDITIONAL flow regime on cross-border disclosure of personal information: before transfer to an overseas recipient, the APP entity must take reasonable steps to ensure the recipient does not breach Australian Privacy Principles. This is a condition precedent to transfer—the entity cannot disclose without first meeting this safeguard requirement. The provision is horizontal (applies across all sectors to entities subject to the Privacy Act) and covers PERSONAL data generally. Under 6.4 scoring tree, this fires the first branch: "The conditional regime covers PERSONAL data — regardless of whether it is horizontal or sector-specific" → score 1. TRAP check (6.1 mirror): this is NOT a ban; a compliant transfer path EXISTS (the entity may transfer if it ensures adequate protection), so 6.4 applies, not 6.1.

mapper.verbatim_quote: The things that may be specified are any of the following that the Attorney ‑ General considers appropriate in the circumstances
mapper.rationale: Warrant authorized by Attorney-General (executive), not a court/independent judicial body, enabling access to data on target computers.

verifier.reason: Section 25A(4) authorizes ASIO to access personal data held in computers without explicit requirement for independent judicial authorization. The warrant is issued by the Attorney-General under s.25A(1)-(2), a political executive official, not a court. The provision enables access to "data...relevant to the security matter" via the Attorney-General's discretionary determination of what is "appropriate"—characteristic of executive-gated access. No court order, judicial warrant, or independent tribunal sign-off is mandated. This directly engages 7.5's first scoring branch: "any measure allows the Government to access (personal) data without a court order / independent judicial authorization...or surveillance authorized by a non-judicial...authority." Scores 1.

mapper.verbatim_quote: to promote the protection of the privacy of individuals with respect to their personal information
mapper.rationale: Privacy Act 1988 is Australia's comprehensive horizontal data-protection framework; objects clause confirms broad, cross-sectoral scope, so lack-of-framework indicator scores 0 (framework exists).

verifier.reason: This provision is s.2A(1) — an objects/preamble clause listing legislative aims. Per Indicator Reference row 80 and the 7.1 coding rule, "Per-provision citations of a data-protection act tagged 7.1 are not discoveries and score zero." Individual provisions of the Privacy Act 1988 are not separate 7.1 discoveries; 7.1 is ECONOMY-LEVEL, answered once per economy by citing the comprehensive act's SCOPE and APPLICATION provision as governing evidence. This objects clause does not establish or evidence the existence/absence of a comprehensive framework — it merely expresses intent. The controlling evidence for AU 7.1 would be the Act's scope provision (defining which entities and data types fall within the framework), not its preamble aims.

escalation.reason: Privacy Act 1988 is AU's comprehensive horizontal DP framework; its objects clause (nationally consistent regulation of privacy/handling of personal information, cross-border flow) evidences existence of the framework → inverted polarity scores 0. Economy-level answer; scope provision ideally cited, but this objects clause supports the framework's existence.

mapper.verbatim_quote: ending 2 years after it came into existence
mapper.rationale: Telecom data retention law sets an explicit minimum retention period of 2 years for metadata, sectoral to telecom providers.

verifier.reason: Section 187C(1) imposes a MINIMUM PERIOD retention requirement: service providers MUST keep telecommunications data for AT LEAST 2 years (measured from account closure or date of creation). This is a specified minimum duration in an enforced statutory regime (TAIA 1979, Part 5-1A). The trap checks: (1) DURATION not LOCATION—correct; this sets a temporal floor, not a storage locus (6.2), so 7.3 applies. (2) MINIMUM not MAXIMUM—the language "ending 2 years after" sets a floor; not a "as long as necessary" cap. (3) SPECIFIED PERIOD—explicitly "2 years"; not a vague "prescribed period." The provision is not applied to government data; it regulates commercial service providers' obligations. Scoring tree: "requirement exists to retain data for at least a specified minimum period (duration in days/months/years explicitly stated...)" → score 1.
